notes.text: That feed — They are said to have fed this people, because it was their duty so to do.

Behold — Even the Jewish doctors, as well as the Christian interpreters, understand this as a prophecy of the Messiah who is called the branch, Isaiah iv, 2; liii, 2. And here, he is called the righteous branch, not only because himself was righteous, but because he maketh his people righteous. Shall execute - Protecting the innocent, and defending his people throughout the world, judging the prince of the world, and by his spirit governing his people.

Judah — During the reign and kingdom of the Messiah the people of God typified by Judah and Israel shall be saved with a spiritual salvation, and God will be a special protection to them. And this - The name wherewith this branch shall be called, shall be, The Lord our righteousness. This place is an eminent proof of the Godhead of Christ, he is here called Jehovah, and what is proper to God alone, namely to justify, is here applied to Christ. He who knew no sin, was made sin, (that is, a sacrifice for sin) for us, that we might be made, the righteousness of God in him.

glossa.text: *Woe to the pastors,* etc. ((HIER.)) Because all hope of the Jewish kingdom has failed, he passes over to the princes of the Church; and, the synagogue with its own pastors being forsaken and condemned, the word is made to the apostles, of whom it is said, *I will raise up over them pastors ((Ezech. XXXIV))*, etc.

*Behold the days come, saith,* etc. ((ID.)) The pastors of the synagogue being cast off, that is to say the Scribes and the Pharisees, and the apostles being put in their place, Christ the pastor of pastors is brought in.

notes.text: A horn — Signifies honour, plenty, and strength. A horn of salvation - That is, a glorious and mighty saviour.
His prophets, who have been since the world began — For there were prophets from the very beginning.

To serve him without fear — Without any slavish fear. Here is the substance of the great promise. That we shall be always holy, always happy: that being delivered from Satan and sin, from every uneasy and unholy temper, we shall joyfully love and serve God, in every thought, word, and work.
And thou, child — He now speaks to John; yet not as a parent, but as a prophet.

To give knowledge of salvation by the remission of sins — The knowledge of the remission of our sins being the grand instrument of present and eternal salvation, Heb. viii, 11, 12. But the immediate sense of the words seems to be, to preach to them the Gospel doctrine of salvation by the remission of their sins.
The day spring — Or the rising sun; that is, Christ.

glossa.text:
*Blessed.* Who, while he besought the goodness of God, was given a forerunner in place of deliverance.

*He hath visited.* What he had known was shortly to be done, he relates after the manner of the prophets as though it were already done.

*A horn of salvation to us. ((BEDA.))* By the horn, which rises above the flesh, since all the bones are covered with flesh, the kingdom of Christ is signified, by which the world and the joys of the flesh are overcome. In figure of which David and Solomon were consecrated to the glory of the kingdom with a horn of oil, as Saul before them with a vial.

*Salvation from our enemies, and from the hand,* etc. He hath raised up for us salvation from our enemies; and it is an explanation of the earlier verse, in which he had briefly set the same thing before: *And he hath raised up a horn of salvation to us.*

*To perform mercy to our fathers, and to remember his testament,* etc. He hath spoken, and hath raised up salvation for us, to perform mercy: that the mercy which he promised to the fathers he may fulfil in us, and that the oath which he made to the fathers concerning our deliverance may be accomplished in us through Christ.

*And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest: for thou shalt go before the face of the Lord to prepare,* etc. ((BEDA.)) It is no wonder if he addresses an infant of eight days, etc., *as far as* which he acknowledged that he had received among his sons.

*To direct our feet into the way of peace. And the child grew,* etc. That in all things the steps of our works may accord with the grace of him who enlightens us, until we enter into the dwelling of perpetual peace.

notes.text: Strengthened unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness — This is the highest point: not only to know, to do, to suffer, the whole will of God; but to suffer it to the end, not barely with patience, but with thankful joy.
Who, by justifying and sanctifying us, hath made us meet for glory.
Power detains reluctant captives, a kingdom cherishes willing subjects. His beloved Son — This is treated of in the fifteenth and following verses.

In whom we have redemption — This is treated of from the middle of Colossians i, 18. The voluntary passion of our Lord appeased the Father's wrath, obtained pardon and acceptance for us, and, consequently, dissolved the dominion and power which Satan had over us through our sins. So that forgiveness is the beginning of redemption, as the resurrection is the completion of it.

Who is — By describing the glory of Christ, and his preeminence over the highest angels, the apostle here lays a foundation for the reproof of all worshippers of angels. The image of the invisible God - Whom none can represent, but his only begotten Son; in his divine nature the invisible image, in his human the visible image, of the Father. The first begotten of every creature - That is, begotten before every creature; subsisting before all worlds, before all time, from all eternity.

For — This explains the latter part of the preceding verse. Through implies something prior to the particles by and for; so denoting the beginning, the progress, and the end. Him - This word, frequently repeated, signifies his supreme majesty, and excludes every creature. Were created all things that are in heaven - And heaven itself. But the inhabitants are named, because more noble than the house. Invisible - The several species of which are subjoined. Thrones are superior to dominions; principalities, to powers. Perhaps the two latter may express their office with regard to other creatures: the two former may refer to God, who maketh them his chariots, and, as it were, rideth upon their wings.

And he is before all things — It is not said, he was: he is from everlasting to everlasting. And by him all things consist - The original expression not only implies, that he sustains all things in being, but more directly, All things were and are compacted in him into one system. He is the cement, as well as support, of the universe. And is he less than the supreme God?

And — From the whole he now descends to the most eminent part, the church. He is the head of the church - Universal; the supreme and only head both of influence and of government to the whole body of believers. Who is - The repetition of the expression { Colossians i, 15} points out the entrance on a new paragraph. The beginning - Absolutely, the Eternal. The first begotten from the dead - From whose resurrection flows all the life, spiritual and eternal, of all his brethren. That in all things - Whether of nature or grace. He might have the preeminence - Who can sound this depth?
For it pleased the Father that all fulness — All the fulness of God. Should dwell in him - Constantly, as in a temple; and always ready for our approach to him.

Through the blood of the cross — The blood shed thereon. Whether things on earth - Here the enmity began: therefore this is mentioned first. Or things in heaven - Those who are now in paradise; the saints who died before Christ came.

glossa.text: *In all virtue.* You, I say, strengthened by God in all virtue, namely chastity and the rest. Which he can well do who is the brightness of the Father, that is, the Son. Or according as he has given you clear knowledge.

*Giving thanks.* Now he begins to say that the law does not profit but harms, and that Christ suffices for all good things: which can be known from this, that he himself and the other apostles (who had been in the observances of the law), having dismissed them, fled for refuge to Christ: As if he should say: We pray for you, giving thanks to God, for this reason, because he makes us worthy, which the law never could.

 *He has made us worthy.* Not in the law, but *in the light,* that is, through God who is light of light, by whose grace we are illumined. Or *in the light,* that is, in clear knowledge, from which he who turns aside falls into darkness. *Of the lot.* The will of God is the lot in the human race, with whom there is no iniquity, but he does all things by justice, though a hidden one.

*He has snatched us from the power.* That is, from hell, in which we were held by the devil: as much from our own transgression as from Adam's. *And has translated,* etc. When, raising us from the depth of Tartarus, he brought us into heaven with his only Son. For now believers, who are devoted with fixed mind, going forth from the world, are brought into heaven with an angel of the Father's right hand for their guide. *The kingdom of the Son.* Of which he himself says: *My kingdom is not of this world;* he did not say: It is not here, but, *it is not hence,* because he does indeed sojourn in the world, but is not of the world. For to his own kingdom he says, *You are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world.* They were of the world, when they belonged to the prince of the world.

*Redemption.* The power of the devil being destroyed, the means of liberty was given to us by the pouring out of the blood of him who had no sin. So that, because the devil justly held those whom, guilty of sin, he had bound by the condition of death, he might justly let these go through him whom, guilty of no sin, the punishment of death undeservedly visited.

*Who is the image.* In one way the image of a king is in a coin, in another in a son. We are the coin, in whom the image of God is Christ the Son. No image of God ought to be worshipped, save that which is the very thing that he himself is, nor is that image to be worshipped instead of him, but with him.

*The head of the body, the Church.* Because he stands to the Church as the head to the body. And since the Church began from Abel, how is he their head? Rightly, because he is the beginning of the Church, that is, its founder. *Who is the beginning.* Of the Church according to the divinity, that is, the founder of the Church, because he has illumined all the just, who from Abel as far as the last just man are begotten, by the power of his divinity and by the gift of his mercy. According to the humanity also he can be called the beginning of the Church, because it is founded upon the faith of his humanity. And rightly is he himself head and beginning, and ruler, and founder, because he himself is the firstborn, etc. *The firstborn,* etc. As he was born before all things of God, that he might create all things, so as man he first rises again, that he may restore, that he may always be first and chief.
*The fulness.* Because he can do all things of himself; whence: *As the Father has life in himself, so also the Son, who raises up and quickens whom he will,* thus he is shown to be perfect God.

*To reconcile through him.* It pleased God to reconcile through him, and he himself made peace not gratuitously, but through blood, things heavenly and things earthly, whence entrance into heaven lies open to man. *All things,* made through him, live in him their author.

notes.text: Then said Jesus — Our Lord passed most of the time on the cross in silence: yet seven sentences which he spoke thereon are recorded by the four evangelists, though no one evangelist has recorded them all. Hence it appears that the four Gospels are, as it were, four parts, which, joined together, make one symphony. Sometimes one of these only, sometimes two or three, sometimes all sound together. Father - So he speaks both in the beginning and at the end of his sufferings on the cross: Forgive them - How striking is this passage! While they are actually nailing him to the cross, he seems to feel the injury they did to their own souls more than the wounds they gave him; and as it were to forget his own anguish out of a concern for their own salvation. And how eminently was his prayer heard! It procured forgiveness for all that were penitent, and a suspension of vengeance even for the impenitent.
If thou be the Christ; ver. 37. If thou be the king — The priests deride the name of Messiah: the soldiers the name of king.
Matt. xxvii, 37; Mark xv, 26; John xix, 19.

And one of the malefactors reviled him — St. Matthew says, the robbers: St. Mark, they that were crucified with him, reviled him. Either therefore St. Matthew and Mark put the plural for the singular (as the best authors sometimes do) or both reviled him at the first, till one of them felt "the overwhelming power of saving grace."

The other rebuked him — What a surprising degree was here of repentance, faith, and other graces! And what abundance of good works, in his public confession of his sin, reproof of his fellow criminal, his honourable testimony to Christ, and profession of faith in him, while he was in so disgraceful circumstances as were stumbling even to his disciples! This shows the power of Divine grace. But it encourages none to put off their repentance to the last hour; since, as far as appears, this was the first time this criminal had an opportunity of knowing any thing of Christ, and his conversion was designed to put a peculiar glory on our saviour in his lowest state, while his enemies derided him, and his own disciples either denied or forsook him.

Remember me when thou comest — From heaven, in thy kingdom - He acknowledges him a king, and such a king, as after he is dead, can profit the dead. The apostles themselves had not then so clear conceptions of the kingdom of Christ.
In paradise — The place where the souls of the righteous remain from death till the resurrection. As if he had said, I will not only remember thee then, but this very day.

glossa.text: *The place of Calvary.* Outside the gate of Jerusalem were places in which the heads of the condemned were struck off, and they were called places of Calvary, that is, of the beheaded. There he is crucified, that, there was the ground of the condemned, the standards of martyrdom might be raised up. *And the robbers,* etc. Execrable in the deed is the iniquity of the Jews, which crucifies the Redeemer of all as though a robber; yet in the mystery he is a good robber, who lay in wait for the devil, to carry off his vessels. By him who is on the right hand is signified the mortification of the flesh for heavenly glory; by him who is on the left, the mortification of the flesh for some cause of this world.

*And Jesus,* etc. Because Luke set himself to write Christ's priesthood, rightly does the Lord intercede with God for his persecutors by the right of a priest, and open paradise to the robber who confesses him; nor does he pray in vain, but obtains it for those who believed after his passion. He does not pray for those who through envy and pride understood him to be the Son of God, and deny and crucify him, but for those who, having a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge, knew not what they did.

*Dividing.* Of these John speaks more fully. The fourfold garment signifies the Church, which consists of four parts, spread through the whole world, distributed equally, that is, harmoniously, to all the parts. The tunic allotted signifies the unity of all the parts, which is held together by the bond of charity. *Lots.* In the lot the grace of God is commended. For thus it came in one to all, when the lot pleased all; because the grace of God also comes to all in unity, and when the lot is cast it is credited not to anyone's person or merits, but to the hidden judgment of God.

*He saved others.* By their own sentence they condemn themselves, who even against their will confess that he saved others. He could indeed have saved himself, but because he himself is the Christ, the elect of God, he was unwilling to come down from the cross. For he who came for this, that he might be crucified for us, for this reason neglected to save himself from the cross: because by dying he took care to save, along with the rest of sinners, even those who crucified him.

*And the soldiers also mocked him,* etc. Note that the Jews deride the name of Christ and of the Son of God, handed down to them by the authority of Scripture. But the soldiers, ignorant of the Scriptures, insult not Christ the elect of God, but the king of the Jews. *And offering him vinegar.* Vinegar were the Jews, degenerating from the wine of the patriarchs. With this vinegar the soldiers give the Lord to drink, whom at their prompting they deliver to death.

*And there was also,* etc. These three tongues were pre-eminent above the rest: Hebrew, because of the Jews glorying in the law; Greek, because of the wisdom of the Gentiles; Latin, because of the Romans holding command. Therefore, will they or nill they, the Jews, every kingdom of the world, all worldly wisdom, and all the divine sacraments of the law bear witness that Jesus is the emperor of those who believe and confess him. *This is the king of the Jews.* The title which witnesses that Christ is king is set not below but above the cross, because although on the cross he was suffering in the weakness of a man, yet above the cross he was shining in the majesty of a king; and therefore, when he had been sacrificed, the title was set above him, that it might lie open to all who wished to read, that is, to believe, that through the cross he did not lose his empire but strengthened it.
*He rebuked him.* The rebuke itself reveals the coming scandal of the cross even among believers, of whom some are on the right hand, others on the left.

*Lord, remember me.* Great grace shines out in this robber. He has no member free from the torment except his heart and his tongue; the whole of what he has free, he offers. With the heart he believes, with the mouth he confesses. He had faith, who believed that he would reign whom he saw dying beside him. He had hope, who asked for entrance. He held charity firmly, who both convicted the robber concerning his own iniquity and preached to him the life which he had come to know. Great is his virtue: he confesses him whom he sees dying in human weakness, whom the apostles were denying, whom they had seen working miracles by divine power.

*Amen I say to thee.* A most beautiful example of a conversion to be sought after, in that pardon is so quickly loosed to the robber, and the grace is more abundant than the petition. For the Lord always bestows more than he is asked. He was asking: *Remember me,* etc. The Lord says: *This day thou shalt be with me,* etc. Quickly does the Lord pardon, because that man is quickly converted.

notes.text: Though — Though there should be nothing but confusion, and desolations round about us: which are often expressed by such metaphors.

A river — This may design the gracious presence, and blessing of the Lord, which is frequently described under the name of waters. Make glad - Shall not barely preserve it from danger, but give great occasion for rejoicing and thanksgiving. The city - Jerusalem, the place where God's holy tabernacle is settled.
Raged — Against God, and against his people. Uttered - He spake to them in his wrath. The earth - The inhabitants of the earth were consumed.
Desolations — Among those who were vexatious to God's people.
To cease — He hath settled as in a firm and well-grounded peace. The land - Of Israel: from one end of it to the other. The bow - The bows and spears, and chariots of their enemies.

Be still — Stir no more against my people. God - The only true and almighty God; your gods are but dumb and impotent idols. Exalted - I will make myself glorious by my great and wonderful works. This psalm seems to have been composed upon the occasion of carrying the ark from the house of Obed-edom into the city of Zion, 2 Sam. vi, 12, 17. But as Zion was a type of the church, and the ark a type of Christ, so it has a farther reference, even to Christ's ascension into heaven, and to the spreading of his kingdom in all parts of the world. It contains an exhortation to rejoice in God, ver. 1-4. A prophecy of Christ's ascension, and of the calling of the Gentiles, ver. 5-9. To the chief musician, A psalm for the sons of Korah.

glossa.text: *Our God.* ((CASS., AUG.)) In the coming of the Lord all hope is shown to be had, even in the passing over of the Apostles to the Gentiles. *They have found us exceedingly.* ((AUG.)) For we were fleeing them. Or, *they have found us* exposed through Adam. *Exceedingly,* by so much the more powerful is he who delivers.

*The earth shall be troubled, and the mountains shall be removed,* etc. ((CASS.)) Judea, as it were dry land: without idolatry, hemmed about by the bitterness of the Gentiles. Or, *the sea,* ((AUG.)) the world.

*The heart of the sea.* The savagery of the Gentiles

*They have sounded, and are troubled,* etc. Those who contradict, the Gentiles: or the Apostles by preaching.

*And their waters were troubled.* The reference is made to the sense, not to the word: that is, the waters of the sea, namely the peoples, or their doctrines, which have been made foolish, the doctrine of the Saviour flashing forth; whence: *They were swallowed up,* etc. And this is the rod of Moses, which devoured the rods of the Magi.

*The stream of the river.* ((CASS.)) Diapsalmus. Because the Church is founded in Christ, to whom the nations and kingdoms are made subject. ((AUG.)) As if he should say: Thus the sea rages; but amid these waves and noises they fear not, who have fled to that refuge.

*He shall help her.* ((CASS.)) Or, *with his countenance,* that is, by the showing forth of his help, when by helping he declares himself. *In the morning.* In the very beginning of a good work; and this, *at daybreak,* that is, through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, who is light as it were of day.
*He gave.* As it were a great reward. *His voice.* Preaching, at which the earthly man trembled. He shall tremble for fear of the judge.

*The Lord of hosts. ((Ibid.))* Briefly he defines what Christ is. *With us.* As it were: He who sent the angels, now he himself has come, and is with us, because with us as our upholder; therefore: *Come,* as it were I invite you now secure. *Ours.* Not save of the sons of the cross. *The God of Jacob.* Who gave us as great things as he gave Jacob: for he is not the God of him alone.

*Come and see. ((Ibid.))* Diapsalmus. The mighty works of the incarnation. *He hath set.* As it were signs, for the calling of the people. *Prodigies.* As concerning the birth from the Virgin, and the star, and the rest. *Making wars to cease.* ((AUG.)) Because through his coming the idolatry and superstition of the whole world perished, or, at that time for his presence the world was at peace.
*Be still. ((Ibid.))* If the arms are burnt up, *be still,* not having wherewith you may fight.

glossa.text: *In all virtue.* You, I say, strengthened by God in all virtue, namely chastity and the rest. Which he can well do who is the brightness of the Father, that is, the Son. Or according as he has given you clear knowledge.

*Giving thanks.* Now he begins to say that the law does not profit but harms, and that Christ suffices for all good things: which can be known from this, that he himself and the other apostles (who had been in the observances of the law), having dismissed them, fled for refuge to Christ: As if he should say: We pray for you, giving thanks to God, for this reason, because he makes us worthy, which the law never could.

 *He has made us worthy.* Not in the law, but *in the light,* that is, through God who is light of light, by whose grace we are illumined. Or *in the light,* that is, in clear knowledge, from which he who turns aside falls into darkness. *Of the lot.* The will of God is the lot in the human race, with whom there is no iniquity, but he does all things by justice, though a hidden one.

*He has snatched us from the power.* That is, from hell, in which we were held by the devil: as much from our own transgression as from Adam's. *And has translated,* etc. When, raising us from the depth of Tartarus, he brought us into heaven with his only Son. For now believers, who are devoted with fixed mind, going forth from the world, are brought into heaven with an angel of the Father's right hand for their guide. *The kingdom of the Son.* Of which he himself says: *My kingdom is not of this world;* he did not say: It is not here, but, *it is not hence,* because he does indeed sojourn in the world, but is not of the world. For to his own kingdom he says, *You are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world.* They were of the world, when they belonged to the prince of the world.

*Redemption.* The power of the devil being destroyed, the means of liberty was given to us by the pouring out of the blood of him who had no sin. So that, because the devil justly held those whom, guilty of sin, he had bound by the condition of death, he might justly let these go through him whom, guilty of no sin, the punishment of death undeservedly visited.

No image of God ought to be worshipped, save that which is the very thing that he himself is, nor is that image to be worshipped instead of him, but with him.

*The head of the body, the Church.* Because he stands to the Church as the head to the body. And since the Church began from Abel, how is he their head? Rightly, because he is the beginning of the Church, that is, its founder. *Who is the beginning.* Of the Church according to the divinity, that is, the founder of the Church, because he has illumined all the just, who from Abel as far as the last just man are begotten, by the power of his divinity and by the gift of his mercy. According to the humanity also he can be called the beginning of the Church, because it is founded upon the faith of his humanity. *The fulness.* Because he can do all things of himself; whence: *As the Father has life in himself, so also the Son, who raises up and quickens whom he will,* thus he is shown to be perfect God.

*To reconcile through him.* It pleased God to reconcile through him, and he himself made peace not gratuitously, but through blood, things heavenly and things earthly, whence entrance into heaven lies open to man. *All things,* made through him, live in him their author.

notes.text: Then said Jesus — Our Lord passed most of the time on the cross in silence: yet seven sentences which he spoke thereon are recorded by the four evangelists, though no one evangelist has recorded them all. Hence it appears that the four Gospels are, as it were, four parts, which, joined together, make one symphony. Sometimes one of these only, sometimes two or three, sometimes all sound together. Father - So he speaks both in the beginning and at the end of his sufferings on the cross: Forgive them - How striking is this passage! While they are actually nailing him to the cross, he seems to feel the injury they did to their own souls more than the wounds they gave him; and as it were to forget his own anguish out of a concern for their own salvation. And how eminently was his prayer heard! It procured forgiveness for all that were penitent, and a suspension of vengeance even for the impenitent.
If thou be the Christ; ver. 37. If thou be the king — The priests deride the name of Messiah: the soldiers the name of king.
Matt. xxvii, 37; Mark xv, 26; John xix, 19.

And one of the malefactors reviled him — St. Matthew says, the robbers: St. Mark, they that were crucified with him, reviled him. Either therefore St. Matthew and Mark put the plural for the singular (as the best authors sometimes do) or both reviled him at the first, till one of them felt "the overwhelming power of saving grace."

The other rebuked him — What a surprising degree was here of repentance, faith, and other graces! And what abundance of good works, in his public confession of his sin, reproof of his fellow criminal, his honourable testimony to Christ, and profession of faith in him, while he was in so disgraceful circumstances as were stumbling even to his disciples! This shows the power of Divine grace. But it encourages none to put off their repentance to the last hour; since, as far as appears, this was the first time this criminal had an opportunity of knowing any thing of Christ, and his conversion was designed to put a peculiar glory on our saviour in his lowest state, while his enemies derided him, and his own disciples either denied or forsook him.

Remember me when thou comest — From heaven, in thy kingdom - He acknowledges him a king, and such a king, as after he is dead, can profit the dead. The apostles themselves had not then so clear conceptions of the kingdom of Christ.
In paradise — The place where the souls of the righteous remain from death till the resurrection. As if he had said, I will not only remember thee then, but this very day.

glossa.text: *The place of Calvary.* Outside the gate of Jerusalem were places in which the heads of the condemned were struck off, and they were called places of Calvary, that is, of the beheaded. There he is crucified, that, there was the ground of the condemned, the standards of martyrdom might be raised up. *And the robbers,* etc. Execrable in the deed is the iniquity of the Jews, which crucifies the Redeemer of all as though a robber; yet in the mystery he is a good robber, who lay in wait for the devil, to carry off his vessels. By him who is on the right hand is signified the mortification of the flesh for heavenly glory; by him who is on the left, the mortification of the flesh for some cause of this world.

*And Jesus,* etc. Because Luke set himself to write Christ's priesthood, rightly does the Lord intercede with God for his persecutors by the right of a priest, and open paradise to the robber who confesses him; nor does he pray in vain, but obtains it for those who believed after his passion. He does not pray for those who through envy and pride understood him to be the Son of God, and deny and crucify him, but for those who, having a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge, knew not what they did.

*Dividing.* Of these John speaks more fully. The fourfold garment signifies the Church, which consists of four parts, spread through the whole world, distributed equally, that is, harmoniously, to all the parts. The tunic allotted signifies the unity of all the parts, which is held together by the bond of charity. *Lots.* In the lot the grace of God is commended. For thus it came in one to all, when the lot pleased all; because the grace of God also comes to all in unity, and when the lot is cast it is credited not to anyone's person or merits, but to the hidden judgment of God.

*He saved others.* By their own sentence they condemn themselves, who even against their will confess that he saved others. He could indeed have saved himself, but because he himself is the Christ, the elect of God, he was unwilling to come down from the cross. For he who came for this, that he might be crucified for us, for this reason neglected to save himself from the cross: because by dying he took care to save, along with the rest of sinners, even those who crucified him.

*And the soldiers also mocked him,* etc. Note that the Jews deride the name of Christ and of the Son of God, handed down to them by the authority of Scripture. But the soldiers, ignorant of the Scriptures, insult not Christ the elect of God, but the king of the Jews. *And offering him vinegar.* Vinegar were the Jews, degenerating from the wine of the patriarchs. With this vinegar the soldiers give the Lord to drink, whom at their prompting they deliver to death.

*And there was also,* etc. These three tongues were pre-eminent above the rest: Hebrew, because of the Jews glorying in the law; Greek, because of the wisdom of the Gentiles; Latin, because of the Romans holding command. Therefore, will they or nill they, the Jews, every kingdom of the world, all worldly wisdom, and all the divine sacraments of the law bear witness that Jesus is the emperor of those who believe and confess him. *This is the king of the Jews.* The title which witnesses that Christ is king is set not below but above the cross, because although on the cross he was suffering in the weakness of a man, yet above the cross he was shining in the majesty of a king; and therefore, when he had been sacrificed, the title was set above him, that it might lie open to all who wished to read, that is, to believe, that through the cross he did not lose his empire but strengthened it.
*He rebuked him.* The rebuke itself reveals the coming scandal of the cross even among believers, of whom some are on the right hand, others on the left.

*Lord, remember me.* Great grace shines out in this robber. He has no member free from the torment except his heart and his tongue; the whole of what he has free, he offers. With the heart he believes, with the mouth he confesses. He had faith, who believed that he would reign whom he saw dying beside him. He had hope, who asked for entrance. He held charity firmly, who both convicted the robber concerning his own iniquity and preached to him the life which he had come to know. Great is his virtue: he confesses him whom he sees dying in human weakness, whom the apostles were denying, whom they had seen working miracles by divine power.

*Amen I say to thee.* A most beautiful example of a conversion to be sought after, in that pardon is so quickly loosed to the robber, and the grace is more abundant than the petition. For the Lord always bestows more than he is asked. He was asking: *Remember me,* etc. The Lord says: *This day thou shalt be with me,* etc. Quickly does the Lord pardon, because that man is quickly converted.

registers.label: Spare
lines: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help.
Jesus, remember us in your kingdom.
In him all things hold together; he is the firstborn from the dead.
Jesus, remember us in your kingdom.
Be still, and know that I am God.
Come, let us worship the King. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Here is a strange throne: a cross, two criminals, a mocking sign that reads The King.
Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.
And from that throne, to a dying thief, the King speaks pardon: today, with me, in paradise.
Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.
This is the one in whom all things were made and in whom all things hold together.
Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.
So we crown him — not with our power but with our need — the crucified and reigning Lord.
Jesus, remember us when you come into your kingdom!
